Mitra, Explained

A Sanskrit-speaking robot friend built on Reachy Mini Lite and a MacBook — fully local, offline after model download. This deck walks through the hardware inside the robot, then explains every component of the voice-to-voice pipeline: what it is, why it exists, and why this particular one was chosen.

I · The hardware II · The pipeline Wake word VAD ASR Language ID LLM + vision Agent Guardrails TTS One turn Option B

01 · part I — the hardware

The body: what the pipeline runs through

Reachy Mini Lite has no computer inside — it is a peripheral. A USB cable carries everything (motor commands, camera frames, audio) to the MacBook, where all models run. The photos that follow were taken during assembly of this unit; they got a second life when the robot's microphone later went quiet — every software check came back clean, the input meter never moved, and Pollen's troubleshooting notes pointed at exactly one connector these photos happened to show. So this tour doubles as a diagnostic map: each stop is labeled with the pipeline component it serves and what to check there when something stops working.

Six of the seven assembly photos are used here; one near-identical angle was left out as a duplicate.

02 · hardware

The Lite board — the robot's only "nervous system"

What it does

Distributes power and bridges USB to a serial motor bus. When the daemon logs Found Reachy Mini serial port: /dev/cu.usbmodem…, this is the board answering. Silkscreen credits: designed for Pollen Robotics × Hugging Face, manufactured by Seeed Studio.

Why it matters to the software

All nine motors hang off one daisy chain (IDs 10–18). One loose connector at the end of the chain is enough for the daemon to refuse startup — Missing motors: ["left_antenna"] is a message about this wiring, not about code.

  • 1
    POWER_INThe motors draw far more current than USB supplies — hence the 7 V / 5 A wall adapter, not just a USB cable.
  • 2
    Coil + capacitorsThe copper-wound inductor and round capacitors form a switching regulator, smoothing incoming power into clean steady voltages.
  • 3
    USB_IN / USB_OUTA USB-C pass-through pair — one cable in, a second connection out, so the robot's link can double as a small hub.
  • 4
    Connectors E / F (GND · 6V8 · DATA)The 3-wire motor bus: one ground, one power, one shared data line chaining all motors instead of wiring each individually.
  • 5
    BUT_A / RSTGeneral-purpose and hardware-reset buttons, for recovering the board without unplugging.
Basics — what's that orange ribbon?
The wide orange strip is a flex cable (FPC/FFC): a flat, bendable ribbon connecting two boards through tight or moving spaces, replacing a wire bundle with one thin strip.

03 · hardware

The same board, flipped — where sound and sight plug in

Mic (ears)

The FPC socket marked MIC takes the microphone flex strip from the head — the start of the listening pipeline (wake word → VAD → ASR). Check first when the robot hears nothing: cable orientation (a flex seated backwards produces exactly "device detected, input meter flat at zero"), then whether the strip is creased or torn. That symptom is what sent us back to these photos.

Camera (eyes)

The small daughterboard (22P, pads marked GND·DP·DM·5V — DP/DM are USB's two data lines) is the interface chip that turns camera and mic signals into the USB devices the Mac sees, including the CoreAudio device macOS lists as "Reachy Mini Audio".

USB (everything)

USB_IN/USB_OUT USB-C ports plus RST/BUT_A service buttons. One cable to the Mac carries audio, video, and motor control.

04 · hardware

The antenna bracket — body language lives here

What it's for

The antennas are pure expression: they perk up when Mitra is listening, droop when it sleeps. Emotion and pose commands from the software end here.

A war story

Being last on the chain makes the left antenna the first casualty of a loose connector. When ID 18 vanished from the bus scan, the fix was reseating a cable on this bracket — a good first place to look if the daemon ever reports a missing antenna motor.

Basics — what's a "bus servo"?
An ordinary hobby servo gets its own dedicated wire back to a controller. A bus servo (here, Dynamixel XL330s) has an ID number and listens on a shared 3-wire line alongside every other motor — the same E/F connectors from the mainboard. That's how one small board independently drives all nine motors without nine separate cables.

05 · hardware

Into the head: one ribbon for the eyes

What's in the shot

The two head shells during assembly. The orange Raspberry Pi camera ribbon runs from the body board up to the green camera board mounted between the two round eye pods.

One board, two round housings

The green board between the pods carries the same 22-pin connector style as the mainboard's interface daughterboard. The spec puts a wide-angle camera and two microphones here, face-forward — camera and mics share one job: pointing what the robot sees and hears at whoever is talking to it. Every capture_image() tool call in Mitra's agent starts at this little green board.

Also in this step

The ribbon is a CSI-style Raspberry Pi camera cable — a standard adopted well beyond Raspberry Pi itself. The microSD card handled here slots into the mainboard, holding the board's own firmware/configuration rather than anything user-facing.

06 · hardware

Inside the head shell — speaker and cable routing

Why the speaker matters

Every reply Mitra speaks — Parler-TTS Sanskrit or the mini app's say voice — is resampled on the Mac and played out through this driver via robot.speaker_play().

Assembly lesson

Cable dressing is not cosmetic: the head is a moving Stewart platform, and every one of these cables flexes with it. Neat routing is what keeps connectors seated through thousands of nods.

07 · hardware

Everything connected — ready to close

What's in the shot

The Lite board mounted in the head shell with all connectors seated: motor bus leads, USB-C loop, mic strip, and the camera ribbon arcing down to the eye board. The assembly manual sits in the background.

The takeaway

This is the whole robot: one board, nine motors, a mic, a camera, a speaker. Everything intelligent about Mitra happens on the laptop — which is exactly what makes the software swappable and the project hackable.

09 · part II — the pipeline

From "hey mitra" to a Sanskrit reply

Mitra's software is a chain of specialists. Sound flows in one end, Sanskrit speech comes out the other, and each stage does one job. The next slides take each component in turn: what it is, why the pipeline needs it, and why this particular one.

StageComponentJob
Wakewhisper-tiny transcript matchnotice "mitra" without burning the laptop
SegmentSilero VADfind where speech starts and stops
TranscribeWhisper large-v3-turbo (MLX)turn the utterance into text
Routelanguage detectortag input as English / Kannada / Sanskrit
Think + seeQwen3-VL 8B via Ollamaunderstand, look through the camera, compose Sanskrit
ActStrands agent + toolslet the model capture images, nod, end the session
Verifylexicon + Devanagari validatorguarantee correct, Sanskrit-only output
SpeakIndic Parler-TTS (MPS)read the reply aloud through the robot

10 · component

Wake word — the doorbell

What it is

A small always-on listener whose only job is to notice the word "mitra" and wake the rest of the pipeline. Everything upstream of it stays asleep.

Why it's needed

Running an 8-billion-parameter model against every sound in the room would peg the laptop constantly. A conversational robot needs a cheap gate in front of the expensive machinery — the same pattern as "Hey Siri" or "Alexa".

Why this one

Today the gate is TranscriptWakeDetector: whisper-tiny continuously transcribes small chunks and string-matches the phrase. It needed zero training data and worked on day one — for a custom Sanskrit name, that mattered, because no off-the-shelf wake model knows "mitra". The planned upgrade is a purpose-trained openWakeWord model, which is lighter and doesn't spend ASR compute around the clock.

src/audio/wake.py backlog: MITRA-CustomWakeword-2

11 · component

VAD — knowing when you've finished talking

What it is

Voice Activity Detection: a tiny neural network that labels each ~30 ms slice of audio as speech or not-speech. Stringing those labels together turns a live mic stream into discrete utterances.

Why it's needed

The transcriber needs a complete thought, not a firehose. VAD decides "the user started speaking here, stopped there" — Mitra waits for 0.8 s of silence to call an utterance done (and caps it at 15 s), so it neither interrupts you mid-sentence nor waits forever.

Why this one

Silero VAD: about a megabyte, runs faster than real time on CPU, MIT-licensed, fully offline, and the de-facto standard in open-source voice stacks. There was no reason to spend novelty budget here.

src/audio/vad.py

12 · component

ASR — turning sound into text

What it is

Automatic Speech Recognition converts the segmented utterance into written text. It is the boundary between the audio world and the language world.

Why it's needed

The LLM consumes text, not waveforms. Whatever the user said — English, Kannada, or Sanskrit — must become a string before the brain can reason about it. ASR quality caps the whole system: a mis-heard question cannot be well answered.

Why this one

Whisper large-v3-turbo through Apple's MLX framework. Whisper is the strongest open multilingual family and handles English and Kannada well; the turbo distillation is ~6× faster than large-v3 with little accuracy loss; and MLX runs it natively on the M1's GPU — no CUDA required, fully offline. The honest gap: Whisper has essentially no Sanskrit, so spoken-Sanskrit input is the pipeline's weakest link today — that evaluation is its own backlog item.

src/audio/asr.py backlog: MITRA-SanskritASR-3

13 · component

Language detection — the router

What it is

A small deterministic step that tags the transcript as English, Kannada, or Sanskrit — using the script itself (Devanagari vs. Kannada vs. Latin) plus the hint Whisper emits.

Why it's needed

Mitra understands three languages but always replies in Sanskrit — that asymmetry is the product. Tagging the input ([lang=…]) tells the LLM what it's reading, which measurably improves its handling of code-switched questions from kids.

Why this one

Script inspection is free, instant, and can't hallucinate; no ML model earns its keep for a three-way decision where two languages use distinct alphabets.

src/language_detector.py

14 · component

The brain — a vision LLM, running at home

What it is

Qwen3-VL 8B Instruct, served by Ollama on localhost:11434. A multimodal model: it reads the tagged transcript and looks at camera frames, then composes the Sanskrit reply.

Why it's needed

This is where "conversation" happens — following context across turns, deciding to look when a child holds something up, naming the object, answering follow-ups. Vision built into the same model means no separate object-detector stage to maintain.

Why this one

Three reasons, recorded as a design decision: it has native tool-calling in Ollama (Gemma 3, the runner-up, doesn't — and tool-calling is how the model drives the camera and gestures); at 8B it fits the M1 Max alongside the whole speech stack; and its Indic-language coverage includes usable Sanskrit. Two gotchas worth repeating: use the :8b-instruct tag (the bare :8b is the "thinking" variant — it burns the latency budget and returns empty replies), and verify ollama ps says 100% GPU.

qwen3-vl:8b-instruct Ollama · localhost:11434

15 · component

The agent — giving the brain hands

What it is

The Strands Agent SDK wraps the LLM in an agentic loop with four custom tools: capture_image, speak_sanskrit, nod, and end_session. The model doesn't just answer — it can look, gesture, and end the conversation by calling them.

Why it's needed

Without tools, "what am I holding?" is unanswerable — the model must be able to decide, mid-reply, to grab a camera frame. An agent framework handles that call-tool-then-continue loop, the part that's tedious and error-prone to hand-roll.

Why this one

Core strands, deliberately not the strands-robots lab package — that targets LeRobot manipulation arms with VLA policies, none of which exists for Reachy Mini. Instead, robot actions are plain @tool functions over the official reachy-mini SDK. Strands also makes Option B nearly free: swapping OllamaModel for a cloud provider is a config change, not a rewrite.

src/agent/agent.py src/agent/tools.py

16 · component

Guardrails — trust, but verify (deterministically)

What they are

Two checks between the model and the speaker. The lexicon: a small database of human-verified Sanskrit object names that always overrides whatever the model generated. The Devanagari validator: every reply must pass a script check before it may be spoken.

Why they're needed

An 8B model will occasionally produce a wrong word or drift into Hindi or English — acceptable in a chatbot, not in a tool that children learn language from. Correctness is enforced outside the model, in deterministic code the model cannot talk its way around. (One deliberate exception: turns the orchestrator tags [explain_in_english] — an explicit user request — skip the script check for that single reply.)

Why this design

Verified data beats generated data: the 53-entry seed lexicon is awaiting review by a Sanskrit expert, and once an entry is verified it wins forever. Cheap, auditable, and it converts every human correction into a permanent accuracy gain.

src/validator.py data/lexicon.db backlog: MITRA-LexiconReview-4

17 · component

TTS — the voice, and why it's gated

What it is

Text-to-Speech renders the validated Devanagari reply as audio, which plays through the robot's speaker. Mitra uses Indic Parler-TTS, running on the Mac's GPU (MPS).

Why it's needed

The users are children learning by ear — pronunciation is the pedagogy. The TTS decides whether every syllable the lexicon fought for is actually heard correctly.

Why this one

It's one of very few open models with published Sanskrit support and evaluation, and it's description-conditioned: the voice is steered by a sentence ("a cheerful young child speaker…" in config.yaml) rather than a fixed speaker ID — that's how Mitra got a child's voice without training anything. It's gated on Hugging Face, so a one-time free license acceptance + hf auth login is part of setup (screenshot shows the goal state). If Parler is unavailable, Mitra falls back to an ungated Hindi VITS voice — intelligible, but approximate — and a dedicated Sanskrit fine-tune (Orpheus-3B) is queued for a bake-off.

src/speech/tts.py ai4bharat/indic-parler-tts backlog: MITRA-SanskritTTS-1

One turn, end to end

19 · the escape hatch

Option B — same skeleton, cloud brain

Local-first is a hard requirement — the robot must work with Wi-Fi off. But the architecture keeps one deliberate escape hatch: because the agent layer is Strands, the local OllamaModel can be swapped for a cloud provider (Anthropic, Bedrock) with a config change, disabled by default.

The privacy line holds in both options: raw microphone audio never leaves the laptop. Only the transcribed text (and, when the model asks to look, a camera frame) would go to a cloud model.
